text:
Sasha: Kicking off Aurelia POC  customer wants Private/VPC deployment with strict allowlists. Top asks: keep original client IP for logging and rate-limits, no TLS MITM, and a predictable egress IP for their firewalls. Can we give a short set of recommended topologies + firewall snippet they can hand to their network team?

Mike: TL;DR options we should surface:
- VPC Peering / Transit Gateway (preserves client src IP end-to-end)
- Interface VPC Endpoint (PrivateLink) into our service VPC (cross-account, lower blast radius)
- NLB with proxy-protocol or a managed egress proxy (lets service see client IP while keeping TLS termination choices)

Elaine: Quick nuance: PrivateLink traffic originates from endpoint ENIs in our VPC, so the service sees those ENI addresses. If they MUST see the original client IP, peering or proxy-protocol is needed. PrivateLink is easier for orgs that don't want peering config.

Raj: For peering, what minimal firewall rules do we ask them to add?

Sasha: Here's a concise allowlist they can paste into a ticket to their NetOps (replace CIDRs/EIPs we’ll give during setup):

Sasha: ```text
Outbound allow from on-prem / spoke VPC -> Redwood service:
- Protocol: TCP
- Ports: 443 (HTTPS) outbound to service subnets
- Example dest CIDRs (replace): 10.200.16.0/24, 10.200.17.0/24
- Note (peering): maintain routing for those CIDRs; do NOT NAT source IP if you need original client IP preserved
- Note (if using egress proxy/NAT): allow outbound to our static EIP(s) we will provide (TCP 443)
```

Mike: If they prefer TLS end-to-end and still need client IP, NLB + proxy-protocol setup suggestion:

Mike: ```text
- Deploy an internal NLB (TCP) in front of the inference service
- Enable Proxy Protocol v2 on the NLB target group
- App/runtime must be able to parse proxy-protocol headers for original IP
- Security groups: client->NLB: 443, NLB->target: 443; health checks allowed from NLB
```

Elaine: Cost snippet for the quote: PrivateLink endpoints incur hourly + per-GB data processing fees. NAT Gateway / egress proxies have per-hour + per-GB egress charges. Peering via Transit Gateway may have lower incremental data fees but requires cross-account route setup and possible TGW costs. We should include a delta table.

Raj: Customer asks about session affinity (sticky sessions) for model routing  does that change our recommendation?

Elaine: Affinity is LB-level. If they need source-IP affinity, peering or preserving client IP is required. If using PrivateLink, we can recommend an internal NLB on our side with sticky cookies or source-based affinity to keep a client sticky to the same backend.

Sasha: Short security-questionnaire friendly answer we can paste: 
Sasha: "Redwood supports Private deployments via VPC Peering, Transit Gateway, or AWS PrivateLink. Peering preserves original client IP. PrivateLink provides strong isolation with endpoint ENIs; traffic will appear from endpoint IPs. For clients requiring original IP visibility, we recommend peering or an NLB with proxy-protocol. We provide precise CIDRs and optional static EIPs during onboarding for allowlisting."

Mike: Also callout: if they absolutely forbid TLS interception, we can do TLS passthrough at the NLB and terminate within the service; proxy-protocol still works for IP pass-through on TCP-level LBs.

netops-bot: Onboarding checklist: https://internal.redwood/privatedeploy-playbook  has required IAM roles, KMS/HSM options, CIDR handoff flow, and contact for TGW setup.

Sasha: Next steps: 1) I will get concrete CIDRs + EIPs from infra and share with Aurelia, 2) Mike will produce a quick cost delta (peering vs privatelink vs nat) by EOD, 3) Elaine will draft SG/route table examples and a tiny runtime note on enabling proxy-protocol parsing. Anything else?

Raj: I'll ask Aurelia which of the three constraints is non-negotiable (client IP vs no mitm vs single egress IP) and circle back.

Sasha: Perfect. Ill follow up with the customer after we have the ranges and the cost table. Thanks all!"
